title: Vector Clocks & Lamport Timestamps
description: Learn how distributed systems track causality without synchronized clocks — using Lamport timestamps and vector clocks to detect concurrent events.

segments.text: In a distributed system, there's no global clock. Machine A's clock might be two seconds ahead of machine B's. So how do you figure out which event happened first? That's the problem logical clocks were invented to solve.

Physical clocks drift. Even with NTP synchronization, clocks can be off by milliseconds or more. If server A timestamps a write at 10:00:00.001 and server B timestamps one at 10:00:00.002, you can't be sure which actually happened first.

Leslie Lamport introduced the 'happened-before' relation. Event A happened before event B if A could have caused B. This happens in two ways: they're on the same machine and A came first, or A sent a message that B received.

A Lamport timestamp is a simple counter. Each process increments it before every event. When sending a message, attach the counter. When receiving, set your counter to the max of yours and the message's, then increment. This preserves causal order.

But Lamport timestamps have a critical limitation. If timestamp A is less than timestamp B, we know A didn't happen after B. But we can't tell if A happened before B or if they were concurrent. The ordering is incomplete.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is it important to know whether two events are concurrent versus one happening before the other?

segments.text: Vector clocks solve this. Instead of one counter, each node maintains a vector — an array of counters, one per node. Node A tracks its own events and what it knows about B and C. This gives us enough information to detect true concurrency.

The rules are simple. Before an event, increment your own position. When sending a message, attach your full vector. When receiving, take the element-wise maximum of your vector and the message's vector, then increment your own position.

To compare two vector clocks: if every element in V1 is less than or equal to the corresponding element in V2, then V1 happened before V2. If some elements are greater and some are less, the events are concurrent. Now you can detect conflicts.
segments.thought_prompt: How would a database use this to detect write conflicts between two replicas?

segments.text: Amazon's original Dynamo paper used vector clocks for exactly this. When two replicas independently modify the same key, the vector clocks reveal the conflict. The system can then ask the application to resolve it or use automatic merge logic.

The downside? Vector clocks grow with the number of nodes. With a thousand nodes, every piece of data carries a vector of a thousand counters. In practice, systems use techniques like pruning old entries to keep vectors manageable.

Lamport timestamps give you partial ordering cheaply. Vector clocks give you full causal ordering at the cost of space. Both are fundamental tools for reasoning about time in distributed systems, where the only truth is the order of messages, not the reading of clocks.
